oven.e: From Middle English oven, from Old English ofn (“oven”), from Proto-West Germanic *ofn (“oven”), from Proto-Germanic *uhnaz, *uhwnaz (“oven”). The modern pronunciation shows a sound change in which Middle English /ɔv/ is changed to /uv/; compare the phonetic development of Coventry and shovel.
oven.g: A chamber used for baking or heating.

over.e: From Middle English over, from Old English ofer, ofor, ouer, from Proto-West Germanic *obar, from Proto-Germanic *uber (“over”), from Proto-Indo-European *upér (“above; over”).
From Middle English over (“riverbank, seashore, brink”), from Old English ōfer (“riverbank, seashore, brink, edge, margin, border”), from Proto-Germanic *ōferaz.

overboard.e: From Middle English overbord, overborde, equivalent to over- + board.
overboard.g: Outside of a boat; in the water.

overcast.e: From Middle English overcasten, equivalent to over- + cast.
overcast.g: A cloud covering all of the sky from horizon to horizon.

overcharge.e: From Middle English overchargen, equivalent to over- + charge.
overcharge.g: To charge (somebody) more money than the correct amount or to surpass a certain limit while charging a bill.

overcome.e: From Middle English overcomen, inherited from Old English ofercuman (“to overcome, subdue, compel, conquer, obtain, attain, reach, overtake”). By surface analysis, over- + come.
overcome.g: To surmount (a physical or abstract obstacle); to prevail over, to get the better of.

overdrive.e: From Middle English overdriven, from Old English oferdrīfan, equivalent to over- + drive.
overdrive.g: To drive too hard, or far, or beyond strength.

overdrive.e: From over- + drive, originally referring to gear ratios over 1:1.
overdrive.g: A gear, on an automobile, higher than the traditional top gear, mainly to allow better fuel economy at highway speeds. In the 21st century,

overflow.e: From Middle English overflowen, from Old English oferflōwan, equivalent to over- + flow.

overhead.e: From Middle English owerheved, over-hed, over hede (adverb), from Old English oferhēafod (adverb), equivalent to over- + head. Piecewise doublet of overchief.
overhead.g: Located above, especially over the head.

overhead.e: (Sense 1) Abbreviation of overhead projector. : (Sense 2) Back-formation from overhead projector.

overhear.e: From Middle English overheren, from Old English oferhīeran (“to overhear, hear, disobey, disregard, neglect”), equivalent to over- + hear.
overhear.g: To hear something that was not meant for one's ears.

overlap.g: To extend over and partly cover something.

overlay.e: From Middle English overleyen, from Old English oferleċġan, from Proto-West Germanic *obarlaggjan, from Proto-Germanic *uberlagjaną, equivalent to over- + lay.
overlay.g: To lay, spread, or apply (something) over or across (something else); to overspread.

overlive.e: From Middle English overliven, from Old English oferlibban (“to survive”), equivalent to over- + live.

overlook.e: From Middle English overloken. From Middle English overloken; equivalent to over- + look.
overlook.g: A vista or point that gives a view down toward something else.

overly.g: Superficial; not thorough; careless, negligent, inattentive.

overmuch.e: From Middle English overmuche, overmuchel, from Old English ofermiċel, ofermyċel (“overmuch, excessive”), equivalent to over- + much.
overmuch.g: Very much; too much; overly much.

overmuch.e: From Middle English overmuche, overmuchel, equivalent to over- + much.

overnight.e: From Middle English overnyght, from Old English ofer niht (“through the night, overnight”), equivalent to over + night. Verbal use (late 19th c.) may have been influenced by German übernachten (16th c.), though it could also have developed independently.
overnight.g: During or throughout the night, especially during the evening or night just past.

overpast.g: ended; having passed over or passed by

overplus.e: From over- + Anglo-Norman plus, Middle French plus.
overplus.g: That which remains beyond what is necessary or required; a surplus.

oversee.e: From Middle English overseen, ouverseen, from Old English ofersēon (“to observe, oversee; to overlook, neglect”), equivalent to over- + see.
oversee.g: To survey, look at something in a wide angle.

overshadow.e: From Middle English overschadwen, overschadewe, from Old English ofersċeadwian (“to overshadow”), equivalent to over- + shadow.
overshadow.g: To obscure something by casting a shadow.

oversight.e: From over- + sight. Verb sense 2 is a semantic loan from German Aufsicht.
oversight.g: An omission; something that is left out, missed, or forgotten.

overspread.e: From Middle English overspreden, from Old English ofersprǣdan; equivalent to over- + spread.
overspread.g: To spread over or across (something); cover over; be scattered over; permeate, overrun.

overstep.e: From Middle English *oversteppen, from Old English ofersteppan, from Proto-Germanic *uberstapjaną (“to step over; overstep”). By surface analysis, over- + step.
overstep.g: To go too far beyond (a limit); especially, to cross boundaries or exceed norms or conventions.

overtake.e: From Middle English overtaken, likely a replacement alteration (as the Middle English verb taken replaced nimen (“to take”)), of Middle English overnimen (“to overtake”), from Old English oferniman (“to take by surprise, overtake”), equivalent to over- + take.
overtake.g: To pass a slower moving object or entity (on the side closest to oncoming traffic).

overthrow.e: From Middle English overthrowen, equivalent to over- + throw. For the noun sense, compare Middle English overthrow, overthrowe (“destruction, downfall”), from the verb.
overthrow.g: To bring about the downfall of (a government, etc.), especially by force; to usurp.

overturn.e: From Middle English overturnen, equivalent to over- + turn.
overturn.g: To turn over, capsize or upset.

overwhelm.e: From Middle English overwhelmen, equivalent to over- + whelm.
overwhelm.g: To engulf, surge over and submerge.
